```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(httr2)
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 10))

set.seed(664)  # Only matters if we add simulation or bootstrap steps.

start_date <- as.Date("2000-01-01")
end_date <- as.Date("2026-09-01")
```

```{r}
#| label: load-data
#| include: false

# Same data pipeline as the plan (STOR_664_Project.qmd).
# Download the publicly available French data archives.

base_url <- paste0(
  "https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/",
  "faculty/ken.french/ftp/"
)

download_french <- function(filename) {
  destination <- tempfile(fileext = ".zip")

  request(paste0(base_url, filename)) |>
    req_user_agent("Mozilla/5.0") |>
    req_perform(path = destination)

  extraction_dir <- tempfile()
  dir.create(extraction_dir)

  files <- unzip(destination, exdir = extraction_dir)

  csv_file <- files[
    grepl("\\.csv$", files, ignore.case = TRUE)
  ][1]

  readLines(csv_file, warn = FALSE)
}

# Extract the monthly table, excluding annual summaries.

read_monthly <- function(lines) {
  monthly <- grepl("^\\s*[0-9]{6}\\s*,", lines)

  first <- which(monthly)[1]
  last <- first

  while (last < length(lines) && monthly[last + 1]) {
    last <- last + 1
  }

  block <- lines[c(first - 1, first:last)]

  result <- read.csv(
    text = paste(block, collapse = "\n"),
    check.names = FALSE,
    strip.white = TRUE
  )

  names(result)[1] <- "ym"
  result$ym <- as.character(result$ym)

  result
}

industry_raw <- read_monthly(
  download_french("5_Industry_Portfolios_CSV.zip")
)

factors_raw <- read_monthly(
  download_french("F-F_Research_Data_Factors_CSV.zip")
)

# Retain monthly returns, reported in percentage points.

industry <- industry_raw |>
  select(ym, Cnsmr, Manuf, HiTec, Hlth, Other)

factors <- factors_raw |>
  select(ym, `Mkt-RF`, RF)

data <- inner_join(industry, factors, by = "ym") |>
  mutate(
    date = as.Date(paste0(ym, "01"), format = "%Y%m%d"),
    market = `Mkt-RF`,
    health = Hlth - RF,
    negative = as.integer(market < 0),
    interaction = market * negative
  ) |>
  filter(
    date >= start_date,
    date <= end_date,
    if_all(
      c(Cnsmr, Manuf, HiTec, Hlth, Other, market, RF),
      ~ is.finite(.x) & .x > -99
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(date)

n_negative <- sum(data$negative == 1)
n_nonnegative <- sum(data$negative == 0)

# TODO: If we pin the sample to a fixed end date for reproducibility
# (the French library updates monthly), add e.g.
#   end_date <- as.Date("2026-09-01")
# to the setup chunk and filter(date <= end_date) here.
```

```{r}
#| label: main-models
#| include: false

# Primary models from the plan.

model_simple <- lm(health ~ market, data = data)

model_asymmetric <- lm(health ~ market + interaction, data = data)

beta_positive <- unname(coef(model_asymmetric)["market"])

beta_negative <- unname(
  coef(model_asymmetric)["market"] +
    coef(model_asymmetric)["interaction"]
)

slope_difference <- beta_negative - beta_positive  # equals beta_2-hat

# Inference for beta_2 (classical OLS).
beta2_summary <- summary(model_asymmetric)$coefficients["interaction", ]
beta2_ci <- confint(model_asymmetric)["interaction", ]

# Partial F-test comparing the nested models (equivalent to the t-test).
nested_test <- anova(model_simple, model_asymmetric)

n_negative <- sum(data$negative)
n_nonnegative <- nrow(data) - n_negative
```

```{r}
#| label: hac-inference
#| include: false

# Primary inference: Newey-West HAC standard errors.
hac_lag <- 6
z_crit <- qnorm(0.975)

# One helper so every HAC calculation uses the same settings:
# Bartlett weights (NeweyWest default), fixed maximum lag,
# no prewhitening, no small-sample adjustment.
hac_vcov <- function(model, lag) {
  NeweyWest(model, lag = lag, prewhite = FALSE, adjust = FALSE)
}

vcov_hac <- hac_vcov(model_asymmetric, hac_lag)

beta2_hat <- unname(coef(model_asymmetric)["interaction"])

# Robust z-test and 95% CI for beta_2 (normal reference distribution).
beta2_hac_test <- coeftest(
  model_asymmetric, vcov. = vcov_hac, df = Inf
)["interaction", ]

beta2_hac_ci <- coefci(
  model_asymmetric, vcov. = vcov_hac, df = Inf
)["interaction", ]
```

## 1. Introduction

### Question and Motivation

Suppose the stock market rises by 5% in a given month and the healthcare industry rises by 3%. Would we expect healthcare stocks to fall by 3% if the market instead declined by 5%? A standard linear model of market sensitivity assumes that an industry's response is symmetric, meaning its sensitivity to market movements remains constant regardless of whether the market rises or falls. However, there are reasons to question whether this assumption holds in practice.

Behavioral economics provides one possible explanation for asymmetric responses. Under the principle of loss aversion, investors may react more strongly to losses than to equivalent gains, potentially influencing how stock prices respond to negative market conditions. Industry characteristics may also play a role. Healthcare, for example, is often considered a defensive industry because demand for medical services and pharmaceuticals tends to persist during economic downturns. As a result, healthcare stocks may respond less strongly to market declines than to comparable market gains. Conversely, industries more dependent on discretionary spending may be particularly sensitive to negative market conditions.

In financial economics, an industry's market sensitivity is commonly measured using its *beta*, the slope coefficient from a regression of industry excess returns on market excess returns. Excess return refers to an asset's return above the risk-free rate. The standard model assumes a single beta across all market conditions, whereas allowing different slopes for positive and negative market excess returns provides a way to investigate potential asymmetry.

**Our primary research question is whether an industry's sensitivity to market movements differs between periods of positive and negative market excess returns.** We focus initially on healthcare, with comparisons across other industries as an extension. Our objective is to estimate these differences and test whether they are statistically significant, rather than to predict future returns.

### Data

We obtain monthly financial data from the [Kenneth R. French Data Library](https://mba.tuck.dartmouth.edu/pages/faculty/ken.french/data_library.html), combining two publicly available datasets: the *Five Industry Portfolios* and the *Fama–French Research Data Factors*. Both datasets are constructed using stock return data from the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP), covering eligible U.S. stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), American Stock Exchange (AMEX), and NASDAQ.

The *Five Industry Portfolios* dataset provides monthly value-weighted returns for five broad industry groups: consumer, manufacturing, technology, healthcare, and other. Stocks are assigned to these portfolios based on their four-digit Standard Industrial Classification (SIC) codes, using classifications from Compustat or CRSP. Portfolio assignments are updated annually in June, and returns are calculated for the following July through June. Within each portfolio, returns are weighted by market capitalization, meaning larger companies contribute more heavily to the portfolio's performance. Our primary focus is the healthcare portfolio, which includes companies involved in healthcare services, pharmaceuticals, and medical equipment.

The *Fama–French Research Data Factors* dataset provides monthly market excess returns (`Mkt-RF`) and the risk-free rate (`RF`). The market return is calculated as the value-weighted return of eligible U.S. common stocks in the CRSP database, representing a broader equity market than the S&P 500 alone. Market excess return is obtained by subtracting the one-month U.S. Treasury bill return from this market portfolio return. The risk-free rate is based on data from Ibbotson Associates through May 2024 and the ICE BofA US 1-Month Treasury Bill Index beginning in June 2024.

Our primary response variable is healthcare excess return, defined as the healthcare portfolio return (`Hlth`) minus the risk-free rate (`RF`). Our explanatory variable is market excess return (`Mkt-RF`). To examine whether healthcare responds differently to market gains and losses, we construct an indicator equal to one when market excess return is negative and zero otherwise, along with an interaction between the indicator and market excess return. All returns are measured in percentage points.

Our analysis sample contains `r nrow(data)` monthly observations from `r format(min(data$date), "%B %Y")` through `r format(max(data$date), "%B %Y")`, of which `r n_negative` months had negative market excess returns and `r n_nonnegative` had nonnegative ones. We restrict the sample to January 2000 onward to focus on relatively recent financial market conditions while retaining sufficient observations for estimation and hypothesis testing.

To prepare the data, we extract monthly value-weighted industry returns and monthly market factors, excluding annual summaries. We treat missing-value codes in the original files as missing and exclude incomplete observations. The datasets are merged by their year-month identifiers using an inner join, ensuring that industry and market returns correspond to the same month. Automated validation checks confirm chronological consistency, the absence of duplicate or missing monthly observations, and the correct construction of our regression variables.

### Setting of Our Conclusions

Our conclusions concern the relationship between monthly excess returns on value-weighted U.S. industry portfolios and the broader U.S. equity market from January 2000 through September 2026. Our primary analysis focuses on healthcare, with comparisons across consumer, manufacturing, technology, and other industries. Because these portfolios consist of publicly traded U.S. stocks and are weighted by market capitalization, our findings primarily characterize the behavior of broad industry portfolios rather than individual companies. We do not claim that these relationships extend to international markets, daily returns, or future periods. Furthermore, our analysis identifies statistical associations between contemporaneous market and industry returns and does not establish causality or provide evidence of predictive performance.

## 2. Methods

### Models

Let $Y_t$\$Y_t\$\$Y_t\$ denote healthcare excess return and $X_t$ denote market excess return in month $t$. The baseline model is

$$Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_t + \varepsilon_t,$$ {#eq-simple}

and the asymmetric model adds an interaction with the negative-market indicator:

$$Y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_t + \beta_2 X_t \, I(X_t < 0) + \varepsilon_t.$$ {#eq-asymmetric}

## 3. Results

### Main Findings

```{r}
#| label: fig-healthcare
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Healthcare excess returns versus market excess returns, with the fitted asymmetric model (@eq-asymmetric). The slope may differ on either side of zero."
#| fig-width: 5.8

plot_data <- data.frame(
  market = seq(min(data$market), max(data$market), length.out = 300)
)
plot_data$interaction <- plot_data$market * (plot_data$market < 0)
plot_data$fitted <- predict(model_asymmetric, newdata = plot_data)
plot_data$direction <- ifelse(
  plot_data$market < 0,
  "Negative market excess return",
  "Nonnegative market excess return"
)

ggplot(data, aes(x = market, y = health)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.35, color = "gray45", size = 1.2) +
  geom_line(
    data = plot_data,
    aes(x = market, y = fitted, color = direction),
    linewidth = 1,
    inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  labs(
    x = "Market excess return (%)",
    y = "Healthcare excess return (%)",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8),
    plot.margin = margin(2, 2, 2, 2)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-models
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Estimated slopes with Newey–West HAC standard errors (Bartlett weights, maximum lag 6) and 95% confidence intervals."

c_neg <- c(0, 1, 1)  # picks out beta_1 + beta_2
se_hac <- sqrt(diag(vcov_hac))
se_negative_hac <- sqrt(drop(t(c_neg) %*% vcov_hac %*% c_neg))
se_simple_hac <- sqrt(hac_vcov(model_simple, hac_lag)["market", "market"])

estimates <- c(
  coef(model_simple)["market"],
  beta_positive,
  beta_negative,
  beta2_hat
)
ses <- c(se_simple_hac, se_hac["market"], se_negative_hac, se_hac["interaction"])

model_table <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c(
    "Single slope, $\\alpha_1$",
    "Nonnegative-market slope, $\\beta_1$",
    "Negative-market slope, $\\beta_1 + \\beta_2$",
    "Difference, $\\beta_2$"
  ),
  Estimate = unname(estimates),
  `HAC SE` = unname(ses),
  `CI lower` = unname(estimates - z_crit * ses),
  `CI upper` = unname(estimates + z_crit * ses),
  check.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(model_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE, escape = FALSE)
```

### Model Checks

```{r}
#| label: fig-diagnostics
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the piecewise model. (a) Residuals against fitted values. (b) Residuals over time. (c) Autocorrelation of residuals. (d) Autocorrelation of squared residuals. Dashed blue lines mark approximate 95% bounds under no autocorrelation."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-align: center

diag_data <- data |>
  mutate(
    fitted = fitted(model_asymmetric),
    resid = resid(model_asymmetric)
  )

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex = 0.75)

# Residuals vs. fitted: does the spread change with the fitted return?
plot(diag_data$fitted, diag_data$resid,
     xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "(a) Residuals vs. fitted", pch = 16, col = "gray40")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# Residuals over time: are there periods of larger deviations?
plot(diag_data$date, diag_data$resid, type = "l",
     xlab = "Month", ylab = "Residuals", main = "(b) Residuals over time")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# ACF of raw residuals: do positive or negative deviations persist?
acf(diag_data$resid, lag.max = 24, main = "")
title("(c) ACF of residuals", line = 0.8)

# ACF of squared residuals: do large deviations cluster in time?
acf(diag_data$resid^2, lag.max = 24, main = "")
title("(d) ACF of squared residuals", line = 0.8)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-lag-comparison
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Inference for $\\beta_2$ under conventional OLS and Newey–West HAC standard errors with maximum lags of 0, 3, 6 (primary), and 12 months. The point estimate is the same in every row. SE ratio is each standard error divided by the OLS standard error."

se_ols <- sqrt(vcov(model_asymmetric)["interaction", "interaction"])
df_ols <- df.residual(model_asymmetric)

summarize_beta2 <- function(method, se, crit, p) {
  data.frame(
    Method = method,
    SE = se,
    `CI lower` = beta2_hat - crit * se,
    `CI upper` = beta2_hat + crit * se,
    `p-value` = p,
    `SE ratio` = se / se_ols,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

# Conventional OLS: t reference distribution with n - 3 df.
ols_row <- summarize_beta2(
  "Conventional OLS", se_ols,
  crit = qt(0.975, df_ols),
  p = 2 * pt(-abs(beta2_hat / se_ols), df_ols)
)

# HAC at each lag: normal reference distribution.
hac_rows <- lapply(c(0, 3, 6, 12), function(lag) {
  se <- sqrt(hac_vcov(model_asymmetric, lag)["interaction", "interaction"])
  label <- paste0("HAC, lag ", lag, if (lag == hac_lag) " (primary)" else "")
  summarize_beta2(label, se, crit = z_crit, p = 2 * pnorm(-abs(beta2_hat / se)))
})

lag_table <- rbind(ols_row, do.call(rbind, hac_rows))
lag_table$`p-value` <- format.pval(lag_table$`p-value`, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)

knitr::kable(lag_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

### Sensitivity Analyses

```{r}
#| label: influence
#| include: false

dfbetas_beta2 <- dfbetas(model_asymmetric)[, "interaction"]
top_idx <- order(abs(dfbetas_beta2), decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]

influential_months <- data.frame(
  Month = format(data$date[top_idx], "%B %Y"),
  market = data$market[top_idx],
  health = data$health[top_idx],
  dfbetas = dfbetas_beta2[top_idx]
)

refit_row <- function(label, drop_idx = integer(0)) {
  fit_data <- if (length(drop_idx) > 0) data[-drop_idx, ] else data
  fit <- lm(health ~ market + interaction, data = fit_data)
  est <- unname(coef(fit)["interaction"])
  se <- sqrt(hac_vcov(fit, hac_lag)["interaction", "interaction"])
  data.frame(
    Sample = label,
    Months = nobs(fit),
    Estimate = est,
    `HAC SE` = se,
    `CI lower` = est - z_crit * se,
    `CI upper` = est + z_crit * se,
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}

influence_table <- rbind(
  refit_row("Full sample"),
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(top_idx), function(i) {
    refit_row(paste("Omit", influential_months$Month[i]), top_idx[i])
  })),
  refit_row("Omit all three", top_idx)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-influence
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Sensitivity of $\\hat\\beta_2$ to the three months with the largest absolute DFBETAS. Intervals use HAC standard errors (maximum lag 6)."

knitr::kable(influence_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The three most influential months for $\hat\beta_2$ are `r paste(influential_months$Month, collapse = ", ")`, with DFBETAS of `r paste(sprintf("%.2f", influential_months$dfbetas), collapse = ", ")`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-subperiods
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Asymmetric model estimates by subperiod. TODO: confirm the subperiod boundaries."

subperiods <- list(
  "2000–2009" = c(as.Date("2000-01-01"), as.Date("2009-12-01")),
  "2010–present" = c(as.Date("2010-01-01"), max(data$date))
)

subperiod_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(subperiods), function(name) {
  bounds <- subperiods[[name]]
  sub <- data[data$date >= bounds[1] & data$date <= bounds[2], ]
  fit <- lm(health ~ market + interaction, data = sub)
  ci <- confint(fit)["interaction", ]
  data.frame(
    Period = name,
    Months = nrow(sub),
    `Up slope` = unname(coef(fit)["market"]),
    `Down slope` = unname(sum(coef(fit)[c("market", "interaction")])),
    `Difference` = unname(coef(fit)["interaction"]),
    `CI lower` = unname(ci[1]),
    `CI upper` = unname(ci[2]),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))

knitr::kable(subperiod_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```
